messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 71
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Oceania
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Painter
  trauma_type: Terrorism
  pcl5: 48

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Reassurance Seeking: I keep asking others to reassure me that I am okay, Emotion Control: I try hard to control my emotions, Avoid Going Out: Going out
  Memory: Bodily Reenactment: When memories come to mind of what happened, I feel my body is in the same position as when the frightening event occurred., Vivid Memory: My memories of the frightening event are very clear and detailed., Uncontrolled Access: The memory forces its way into my mind when I do not want it to
  Negative Appraisals: Can't Rely on Self: I can't rely on myself, Can't Rely on Others: I can't rely on other people, World is Dangerous: The world is a dangerous place

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Sione, a 71-year-old painter of Oceania heritage, had lived his entire adult life in the same coastal city, a place where he had raised his children and built a modest reputation for his seascapes. He was a man accustomed to solitude, his single status a long-established comfort rather than a recent change. That changed on a Tuesday afternoon in late autumn, when a truck bomb detonated two blocks from his ground-floor apartment. He had been on his way to the hardware store for turpentine. The blast threw him against a brick wall, and he landed in a heap, his left arm pinned beneath his own body. In the ringing silence that followed, he could not move. He lay there, staring at a single shattered piece of green glass on the asphalt, convinced his neck was broken, convinced he was bleeding internally, convinced no one was coming. It took what felt like an eternity for paramedics to reach him, though he later learned it had been only minutes. He had no physical injuries beyond bruising, but something had shifted.

In the months that followed, Sione found that the memory of that Tuesday afternoon had a quality he could not shake. When it came—and it came without warning, often while he was reaching for a paintbrush or stepping off a curb—he was no longer in his living room or on a city street. He was back on the ground, his left arm pinned, his breath short, his body locked in that exact position. He could feel the grit of asphalt against his cheek. The memory was so vivid, so detailed, that he sometimes gasped aloud, and his neighbours began to notice. He tried to control this. He told himself firmly that it was over, that he was safe, that he needed to get a grip. But the more he tried to push the images away, the more forcefully they intruded, often at night when he was trying to sleep. He began to believe that his own mind was unreliable, that he could not trust himself to keep it together. This feeling spread. He had always been a self-sufficient man, but now he found himself calling his daughter several times a day, asking the same questions: "Do you think I'm okay? Do you think I'm losing it?" She reassured him each time, but the reassurance never lasted. He needed to hear it again, and then again.

His view of the world darkened. Before the bombing, Sione had considered his neighbourhood safe, familiar, his own. Now he saw danger everywhere. A parked delivery truck made his chest tighten. A loud engine on the street sent him to the window to check. He began to think that other people were not to be relied upon either—that anyone could be a threat, that the kindness of strangers was a myth. He stopped going out. At first, it was just avoiding the block where the bomb had gone off. Then it was avoiding any street with heavy traffic. Then it was simply not leaving his apartment at all. He stopped buying groceries in person and had them delivered. He stopped walking to the ocean to sketch. His canvases remained blank, stacked against the wall. The turpentine he had been walking to buy that day sat unopened in a bag by the door. His daughter urged him to see a doctor, but he resisted. What could a doctor do? The world was dangerous, he was unreliable, and no one else could be counted on.

What finally brought Sione to seek help was a moment of acute shame. His daughter had come to visit, and when she knocked on his door, he found himself frozen, unable to answer. He stood in the hallway, his hand on the lock, his heart pounding, convinced that if he opened the door, something terrible would happen. He heard her call his name, then her footsteps retreating. He stood there for another twenty minutes, ashamed and exhausted. That night, he called her and told her he needed to talk to someone. He is afraid of what he will find in therapy—afraid that talking about it will make the memories worse, that he will be told he is broken beyond repair. But he is also, for the first time, quietly hoping that someone might show him a way to trust himself again, and to believe that the world outside his door is not still waiting to destroy him.
